nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body: 05/22/90. Thomas Czapla; NOAA SEA Division, Silver Spring, MD.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Gizzard shad
Scientific Name: Dorosoma cepedianum

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class: Osteichthyes
      Order: perciformes
      Family: Clupeidae

Other Common Names - eastern gizzard shad, skipjack, hickory shad, mud shad, sawbelly, jackshad, in Quebec aucun. Occasionally referred to as threadfin shad which has been adopted as the vernacular for Dorosoma petenense (471).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: Little commercial value is given to this fish although it is often taken from freshwater lakes in very abundant quantities at which time it is used for fertilizer or animal feed. An attempt has been made to use it as a food fish for man but is usually rejected because of poor flavor, undesirable texture, and being too bony.

Recreational: Sometimes used as a bait fish but usually does not live long on the hook.

Ecological Role: Important forage fish. Characteristically has a rapid population growth when introduced into new systems. When large populations occur they affect the populations, growth and habitat of primary game fish such as bass (356). Massive die-offs are encountered in the Great Lakes associated with temperature.

Indicator: Population sizes have been used by various state agencies to gauge the management needs of large fresh water lakes (356).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  The populations that exist in the interior of the United States are generally landlocked from the coastal populations. Only the coastal range is considered here. New Jersey and southeastern Pennsylvania to northeastern Mexico.

Within Study Area: From the Rio Grande to Alabama; concentrated around fresher water supplies, i.e. the Mississippi River.

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Generally a pelagic fish near the surface in shallow, quiet waters for all life stages.  Aggregations occur with no true schooling. A spring "run" occurs in the Mississippi prior to the spawning season.
Larvae: As larvae, there is a general movement from surface to mid water with increase in size.
Juvenile: Juveniles slowly make their way to more saline waters with age.
Adult: Adults are concentrated in deeper water in the fall and winter. Adults in salt water migrate upstream to spawn during spring months (251 255 561). The increased abundance in inshore waters during winter months (Nov-Feb) may be due to this upstream spawning movement (10 4) .

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Nektonic in fresh to polyhaline waters in river and coastal bays.

Substrate: Widely distributed over mud bottoms, but also occurs over hard bottom lake shores. Taken over mud, vegetation, rubble, sand, gravel, boulders, and bedrock (500).

nodes.title: Physical/chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature: Juveniles and adults collected from 5.0 to 34.9 C and suffer high mortality rates when temperatures fall to 2.2 C. Populations in cold climates are controlled by winter induced cold kills (55 359 372 561 709).

Salinity: Eggs, larvae and small juveniles limited to freshwater. Juveniles less than 40 mm are found in 1.1 ppt or less (587 694). Larger juveniles, usually greater than 70 mm TL, begin to penetrate brackish and more saline waters (587 193). Adults are euryhaline, but prefer brackish to euhaline waters with the greater abundance occurring below 15 ppt (254 255 561). One study reported captures from 4 to 20 ppt (751). Lethal maximum salinity tolerance for adults occurs at 41.3 ppt (587).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: External fertilization.

Mating/Spawning: Spawning takes place in freshwater from mid-March to late August with peaks in April to June in temperate waters. Second spawn may occur in late summer in some areas. Several individuals of each sex are often involved at the time of gamete release, which usually takes place at midday with rising temperatures that range from 10-28.9 C; most active at 18 C (55 374 367).

Fecundity: Fecundity ranges from 22,400-543,900, but changes with age averaging 59,480 at Age I, 378,990 at Age II and declining to 215,330 at Age VI (55).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg: Demersal and adhesive, sticking to substrate if not covered with detritus. Fertilized eggs are creamy yellow, nearly transparent, and 0.75 mm in size. When eggs are first extruded they are hard and irregularly shaped but become spherical after contact with water. Incubation period is temperature dependent and lasts from 36 h to 1 week. Egg hatching occurs after 95 h at 17 C and 36 hours at 27 C (415 3 6 7 ) .

Larvae: Hatch at around 3.25 mm TL, grow to 20-21 mm TL.

Juvenile: Juvenile stage is reached at ca. 20 mm TL. Juveniles mature in about 2 or 3 years, with some females maturing as soon as 1 year. Average length at maturity 178-279 mm TL.  Greater than 20 mm TL; upstream of brackish water, never enter brackish water until >= 70 mm TL.

Adult: In Florida, gizzard shad averaged ca. 254 mm after the first year, 317.5 mm after the second and 345.4 mm after the third with none surviving to the fourth year. In other areas, particularly temperate freshwater locations, growth is much slower with a life span extending to almost 10 years (471) .

Spawning Strategy:  Mid March to late August, peaks in April to June, in temperate waters. Second spawn may occur in late summer in some areas.

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: During the first few weeks as larvae, primary food items are small animals, such as protozoa, water fleas, copepods and ostracods ( 471 ) . After this initial phase when the intestine has had a chance to develop there is a switch to phytoplankton and algae that remains a part of their diet for life. Adults are selective bottom feeders ( 163 ) . Food items are foraminifera, detritus, and substrate supplemented by sponges, snails, clams, annelids, ostracods, copepods, filamentous algae, seeds, and vascular plant material.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Lowest recorded dissolved 02 concentration where fish were collected was 4.6 ppm (1 0 4) .
